newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: India, Pakistan report progress in peace talks.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan report progress in peace talks.

text.p: Indian and Pakistani negotiators achieved "forward movement" on their second day of peace talks on Saturday, a senior Pakistan Foreign Ministry official said.

Delegations led by Indian Foreign Ministry secretary Salman Haider and his Pakistani counterpart Shamshad Ahmad will try to produce an agreed document at a meeting set for Sunday at the resort of Murree, near Islamabad, said Khalid Salim, acting as spokesman for the talks.
"On the whole there has been a forward movement today," he said.

The two sides decided to set down their proposals in working papers that will form the basis of the agreed document, which will cover mechanisms for future talks between the two neilghbours and arch-rivals.
"The ideas of the two sides on various issues have now crystallised and each side has a much better understanding of the other side's point of view," Salim said without giving details.

Earlier, Haider made courtesy calls on Pakistani President Farooq Leghari and Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif. A Pakistani statement said the two leaders told him that New Delhi should avoid "negative factors" for the success of the talks.

Among what Pakistan calls "negative factors", Leghari and Sharif cited a recent alleged violation of Pakistani air space by an Indian spy plane, alleged deployment of missiles near the border, and a border clash in which a Pakistan army officer was killed. India denies the air violation and missile deployment.

Leghari and Sharif said such events should be avoided in order to maintain a conducive atmosphere for dialogue between the two countries, which have fought three wars since their independence from Britain in 1947.

The statement also quoted Sharif as calling for a reduction of India's forces in the Indian-ruled part of the disputed Himalayan region of Jammu and Kashmir, and for an improvement of the human rights situation there.
"The progress should be uniform on a broad spectrum of Indo-Pakistan issues, including the core issue of Kashmir," Sharif said.

Haider told Sharif that Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral had asked him to assure Islamabad that Delhi wanted to "open a new chapter in the relations between the two countries", according to the Pakistani statement.
Both sides said on Friday after the first session of talks that they hoped to devise a mechanism for future meetings.

Apart from an agreement to pursue the dialogue, little emerged from the first round of talks in Delhi in March, but they paved the way for the two foreign ministers to meet in April and the two prime ministers to get together in May.
An earlier dialogue foundered in 1994 over the issue of Kashmir, two-thirds of which is ruled by India and the rest by Pakistan.
